Typically applies when: Customers create and manage their own user accounts or roles in the product.
Report wording: User entities are responsible for administering access for their own users, restricting access to authorised individuals, and modifying or removing access promptly when it is no longer required.

Typically applies when: Customer admins can grant roles or elevated permissions.
Report wording: User entities are responsible for periodically reviewing their users' access and permissions to confirm they remain appropriate.

Typically applies when: Customers can configure MFA, password rules or session settings.
Report wording: User entities are responsible for enabling and enforcing the authentication settings available to them, such as multi-factor authentication, password requirements and session timeouts, in line with their own security policies.

Typically applies when: Customers connect their own identity provider (SAML/OIDC single sign-on or SCIM).
Report wording: User entities are responsible for securing and maintaining the identity provider they use to access the system, including provisioning and de-provisioning users through it.

Typically applies when: Most services with named user logins.
Report wording: User entities are responsible for ensuring their users keep login credentials confidential, do not share accounts, and report suspected credential compromise.

Typically applies when: The service offers APIs, webhooks or access tokens that customers configure.
Report wording: User entities are responsible for configuring, monitoring, managing and securing their API connections and endpoints, including the storage, rotation and revocation of API keys and tokens issued to them.

Typically applies when: Customers can connect third-party apps, plug-ins or marketplace integrations.
Report wording: User entities are responsible for assessing and approving the third-party applications and integrations they connect to the system, and the data those integrations can access.

Typically applies when: Customers upload, import or send data that the service processes or reports on.
Report wording: User entities are responsible for the accuracy, completeness and timeliness of the data they submit to the system, including through file uploads, APIs and integrations.

Typically applies when: The service is not designed for certain sensitive data (e.g. card or health data).
Report wording: User entities are responsible for determining what data they submit to the system and for not submitting data types the service is not intended to protect, such as payment card or health information, unless agreed in their contract.

Typically applies when: Customers can share content, create public links or invite external users.
Report wording: User entities are responsible for configuring sharing, visibility and permission settings for their content, and for restricting public or external sharing where it is not required.

Typically applies when: Customers control retention settings or request data export or deletion.
Report wording: User entities are responsible for configuring the retention settings available to them and for requesting the export or deletion of their data in line with their own retention obligations.

Typically applies when: The service supports bring-your-own-key or customer-held encryption keys.
Report wording: User entities are responsible for generating, protecting and rotating the encryption keys they hold or control, recognising that loss of these keys may result in loss of access to their data.

Typically applies when: Customers submit personal data about their own staff, customers or end users.
Report wording: User entities are responsible for providing any notices and obtaining any consents required for personal data they submit to the system, and for responding to data subject requests relating to that data.

Typically applies when: Customers export, download or sync data to their own environments.
Report wording: User entities are responsible for protecting data once it has been exported, downloaded or synchronised from the system to their own environments, including backing it up where required.

Typically applies when: Nearly all services.
Report wording: User entities are responsible for promptly notifying the service organisation of any actual or suspected security incident, including compromised credentials, relating to their use of the system.

Typically applies when: Customers can view audit logs, login history or admin activity.
Report wording: User entities are responsible for reviewing the activity and audit logs available to them and investigating unusual activity on their accounts.

Typically applies when: Users access the service from customer-managed devices and networks.
Report wording: User entities are responsible for securing the devices and networks their users use to access the system, including keeping them up to date and protected against malware.

Typically applies when: Customers set up VPNs, private links, firewall rules or IP allowlists to connect.
Report wording: User entities are responsible for configuring and maintaining network controls in their own environment, such as firewalls, IP allowlists, private links and VPN connections used to connect to the system.

Typically applies when: Customers install agents, connectors, SDKs, desktop or mobile apps, or self-hosted components.
Report wording: User entities are responsible for installing, updating and securing any agents, connectors, SDKs or self-hosted components of the system that run in their environment.

Typically applies when: The company deploys devices or hardware at customer premises.
Report wording: User entities are responsible for the physical security of, and network connectivity to, equipment deployed at their premises, and for notifying the service organisation of any damage, loss or tampering.

Typically applies when: Customers build their own workflows, rules, automations or configurations in the product.
Report wording: User entities are responsible for designing, testing and approving changes to their own configurations, workflows and integrations within the system before relying on them.

Typically applies when: Customers rely on the service for business-critical operations.
Report wording: User entities are responsible for maintaining business continuity and disaster recovery plans that address their reliance on the system and the possibility of service interruption.

Typically applies when: Most services.
Report wording: User entities are responsible for ensuring their users use the system in accordance with the terms of service and acceptable use policy.

Typically applies when: Most services.
Report wording: User entities are responsible for keeping their administrative and security contact details current, and for reviewing service notifications, status updates and release notes from the service organisation.

Typically applies when: The product generates text, code, images, summaries or recommendations using AI.
Report wording: User entities are responsible for reviewing and monitoring AI-generated outputs to confirm they are accurate, appropriate and meet their objectives before relying on or acting on them.

Typically applies when: AI outputs inform decisions about people, money, safety or compliance.
Report wording: User entities are responsible for maintaining appropriate human oversight and approval of decisions made using AI outputs, particularly where those decisions affect individuals or have legal, financial or safety impact.

Typically applies when: AI agents can take actions or access connected systems on a user's behalf.
Report wording: User entities are responsible for configuring the permissions, tools and connected systems that AI agents can access, limiting them to what is necessary, and for monitoring the actions agents take on their behalf.

Typically applies when: Users can enter prompts, free text or files into AI features.
Report wording: User entities are responsible for determining what data their users enter into AI features and for restricting confidential, personal or regulated data where their own policies do not permit it.

Typically applies when: Customers can enable or disable AI features, or opt in or out of data use for model improvement.
Report wording: User entities are responsible for configuring the AI feature settings available to them, including enabling or disabling AI features and data-sharing or model-improvement options, in line with their own policies.

Typically applies when: Customers fine-tune models or connect their own documents or knowledge bases to ground AI responses.
Report wording: User entities are responsible for the accuracy, appropriateness and lawful use of data they provide to train, fine-tune or ground AI models, and for testing model behaviour before relying on it.

Typically applies when: Customers use AI features in regulated or higher-risk use cases.
Report wording: User entities are responsible for assessing whether their use of AI features is appropriate for their purposes and complies with the laws, regulations and industry requirements that apply to them.

Typically applies when: Customers expose AI chat, agents or AI-generated content to their own customers.
Report wording: User entities are responsible for informing their own end users, where required, that they are interacting with an AI system or AI-generated content.

Typically applies when: The product generates code, scripts, queries or infrastructure configuration.
Report wording: User entities are responsible for reviewing, testing and approving AI-generated code or configuration before deploying it into their environments.

Typically applies when: Customers connect their own AI provider accounts or API keys (e.g. OpenAI, Azure OpenAI, Amazon Bedrock).
Report wording: User entities are responsible for securing and managing the AI provider accounts and API keys they connect to the system, and for the terms under which that provider processes their data.

Typically applies when: The product includes AI features.
Report wording: User entities are responsible for reporting inaccurate, harmful or unexpected AI outputs or behaviour to the service organisation through the agreed support channels.
